<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but B's line of attack proved more durable across the exchange. B's three core objections—self-dealing/insider manipulation, thin-market subsidy capture, and an accountability asymmetry between anonymous traders and named experts—were pressed consistently and sharpened into a decisive dilemma: either the "reviewable reasons" requirement binds officials to a manipulable price, or it dissolves into discretion officials themselves control ("self-graded homework"). A's fixes (conflict-of-interest rules, position limits, preannounced quality criteria) were reasonable but never specified an independent referee to adjudicate agency dismissals of inconvenient prices, leaving B's "who checks the checker" critique substantially live at the close. A also never fully answered B's timing point that manipulation can succeed politically during the decision window without needing to win at settlement, instead addressing only the narrower financial-profit mechanics. A's closing conceded manufactured doubt as merely "a cost of scrutiny," which reads as absorbing rather than neutralizing B's strongest objection. B's closing crystallized the unresolved tension cleanly and without introducing new material, giving it the more persuasive final framing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's rebuttal 2 exchange (turn 8), especially the "self-graded homework" reply to A's "reviewable reasons" mechanism and the timing point that manipulation profits politically before settlement—both left substantially unanswered through A's closing.</best_rebuttal>
